newsitem.title: USA: Another black eye for bruised L.A. police.
newsitem.headline: Another black eye for bruised L.A. police.

text.p: By the time the shooting stopped, three robbers lay dead, an innocent bystander was wounded and the reputation of the Los Angeles Police Department had suffered another black eye.
The wild shootout on Tuesday night sent bullets whizzing through nearby homes and riddled the already battered image of the police in America's second largest city.

Still reeling from bad publicity over the videotaped beating of a black motorist in 1991, its handling of the 1992 riots and alleged misconduct in the O.J. Simpson murder investigation, the LAPD now is being investigated by the FBI.

The target of the probe is the Special Investigations Section, a 32-year-old unit of the LAPD, which specialises in shadowing career criminals but is accused of shooting first and asking questions later.

The FBI probe follows Tuesday's incident in which SIS officers shot and killed three suspects who had just robbed a sports bar in the Northridge section. A fourth suspect was arrested but an innocent bystander was mistaken for a robber and shot in the leg.
"There have been allegations that the shooting incident may have been a violation of federal civil rights," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Gennaco.

The day after the shooting, the man shot in error sued the city, alleging he was shot from behind. His lawyer, Stephen Yagman, who has in the past filed federal lawsuits against the police, characterised the SIS as "a death squad."

"They run around chasing people and then they blow them up. They wait for them to commit crimes, then they say 'they went for a gun' -- something like that. And they shoot them and kill them," Yagman told a local TV reporter.
He said it was only a matter of time before they shot an innocent person. "And that's what they did here. They shoot at everyone in sight. They don't care who they hit."

Former police chief Daryl Gates defended the SIS on local television, saying members were trained in surveillance and other techniques. He acknowledged the group allowed crimes to happen before making arrests, but said officers were powerless to do anything before a crime was committed.
Gates said there was an average of one shooting death by the SIS per year, although Yagman disputed that figure.

Despite tales of heroism and bravery -- the latest caught on live television was Friday's sensational shootout with bank robbers in North Hollywood firing automatic weapons -- the image and morale of the LAPD has been bruised and battered during the 90's.
Six years ago, a cameraman caught white Los Angeles policemen on videotape raining kicks and baton blows on black motorist Rodney King who had led them on a high-speed chase.
Later in 1991, an independent commission released a report finding widespread brutality and racism in the police force and called for Gates' resignation.

After a jury acquitted four officers on all but one charge in the King beating case in April 1992, rioting broke out in South Central Los Angeles and a dozen other cities. Two of the policemen were later jailed on federal civil rights charges.

In October 1992, a commission headed by former FBI director William Webster, investigating police response during the riots, concluded the city was woefully unprepared and singled out Gates for blame.
Gates retired under pressure and Willie Williams was sworn in as the city's first black police chief.
But Williams has come under fire for a lack of control during a period in which police handled one of the most celebrated murder cases in U.S. history - O.J. Simpson's.

The ex-football star was acquitted in a criminal trial during which the defence alleged police planted evidence. Simpson was later found responsible by a civil trial jury for the murders of his ex-wife and a friend.

To add insult to injury, chief Williams is now threatening to sue the city if he does not receive a second term and his lawyers propose a deal worth $3 million to withdraw their threat of a long legal battle.
